prompt: Your plan says 300 Mbps and your download manager shows about 37 MB/s. What is happening?
hint: Look carefully at the two letters.

choices.text: The connection is delivering roughly an eighth of what was promised
choices.why: Nothing is missing; the two numbers agree once converted.

choices.text: The download manager is measuring after compression has been applied
choices.why: Compression is not what accounts for a factor of exactly eight.

choices.text: The same quantity in the other unit — eight bits to a byte
choices.why: Plans are quoted in bits, downloads counted in bytes.

choices.text: Overheads on the path are consuming seven eighths of the capacity
choices.why: Overheads are a few per cent, not seven eighths.

prompt: A plan is sold as 600 Mbps. About how many megabytes per second is that?
hint: Eight bits make a byte.

prompt: A path runs over links of 1200, 300, 40, 940 and 10000 Mbps. What can the path deliver?
hint: A chain is as strong as which link?

choices.text: About 40 Mbps, because you get the narrowest link
choices.why: The bottleneck belongs to the path, not to your plan.

choices.text: The average of the five, since load is spread across them
choices.why: Traffic crosses every link in turn; it is not spread among them.

choices.text: About 300 Mbps, since that is what the plan was sold as
choices.why: Your plan is only one candidate for the bottleneck, and here it is not it.

choices.text: About 10000 Mbps, because the path can carry that much
choices.why: One enormous link does not lift the ones around it.

prompt: Which of these are true of the number on an internet plan? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read what it promises, and to whom.

choices.text: It is the download figure, and upload is a fraction of it
choices.why: Domestic connections are asymmetric and the second number is printed smaller.

choices.text: It is a maximum rather than a guaranteed rate
choices.why: Up to that figure, in good conditions.

choices.text: It describes how fast a single packet travels to its destination
choices.why: Nothing travels faster on a bigger connection; that is latency.

choices.text: It guarantees what any particular website will send you
choices.why: The other end decides that, and it has other people to serve.

choices.text: It is shared with the other devices in the building
choices.why: One line serves them all.

prompt: On a video call, you see the other person clearly and they say your picture is frozen. What does that point at?
hint: The two directions are not the same size.

choices.text: Your upload, which on a domestic plan is a fraction of your download
choices.why: Their picture uses your large download; yours uses your small upload.

choices.text: The call software has chosen a lower quality for you than it did for them
choices.why: Quality is chosen from what the link delivers, so this is the symptom rather than the cause.

choices.text: Your download, which their incoming video has completely saturated
choices.why: If your download were the problem, their picture would be the broken one.

choices.text: A slow processor too far behind to encode your picture and keep up
choices.why: Possible in principle, but the asymmetry of the plan explains it far more often.

prompt: Which of the four components of latency is a floor that no equipment can lower?
hint: One of them is physics rather than engineering.

choices.text: Processing — each router along the way reading the header and deciding
choices.why: It is small and it does improve with better equipment.

choices.text: Queuing — waiting behind whatever traffic is already at that hop
choices.why: That one is the most variable of the four and can be very largely removed.

choices.text: Propagation — distance at the speed of light in glass
choices.why: Divide the distance by 200,000 km per second and that delay is unavoidable.

choices.text: Transmission — putting the bits onto the wire at that link's capacity
choices.why: That one falls as bandwidth rises.

prompt: A page needs four round trips before its content starts arriving, on a 200 ms link. You double the bandwidth. What happens to those four round trips?
hint: Ask which of them was ever about capacity.

choices.text: They fall by about a quarter, since part of each is transmission
choices.why: Transmission time for a small request is negligible next to the round trip.

choices.text: They halve, since everything on the connection doubles in speed
choices.why: Bandwidth is not speed, and a round trip is not a transfer.

choices.text: Nothing — none of them was limited by capacity
choices.why: Bandwidth shortens the transfer; it does not shorten the waiting.

choices.text: They grow, because more data is now in flight at once
choices.why: More capacity does not lengthen a round trip.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: bandwidth shortens the ___, and latency lengthens ___.
hint: One of them is the short part of a small page load.

prompt: Somebody has enormous bandwidth on a traditional satellite connection and says conversation is exhausting. Why?
hint: The satellite is a long way up.

choices.text: The available bandwidth is shared with everybody under the satellite
choices.why: Sharing affects capacity, and they have more capacity than they need.

choices.text: The connection is asymmetric, so their voice struggles to get out
choices.why: Asymmetry would degrade their audio quality, not add a delay to both sides.

choices.text: The round trip is at least 480 ms before anything else is added
choices.why: 36,000 km up and back twice, which no capacity reduces.

choices.text: Satellite links drop so many packets that a conversation falls apart
choices.why: Loss is not what makes the conversation collide; the delay is.

prompt: Match each component of latency to where it comes from.
hint: Only one of the four is imposed by physics.

pairs.right: Distance, at the speed of light in glass
Putting the bits onto the wire, at that link's capacity
Waiting behind other traffic already at that hop

right_distractors: The receiver holding packets back until the gap is filled
The number of separate connections the browser opened

prompt: What is throughput?
hint: It is measured after the fact.

choices.text: The figure printed on the internet plan
choices.why: That is bandwidth, and it is an upper bound.

choices.text: The time one packet takes to reach the far end
choices.why: That is latency, and it is a different quantity entirely.

choices.text: The rate at which real data actually moved
choices.why: Always below the bandwidth, and the gap is what the section is about.

choices.text: The capacity of the narrowest link on the path
choices.why: That is a ceiling on throughput, not throughput itself.

prompt: A 1 Gbps link with a 200 ms round trip carries a single transfer using a 64 kB window. Why does it reach nowhere near 1 Gbps?
hint: Think about what the sender does after sending 64 kB.

choices.text: A link that long carries less than its stated figure suggests it would
choices.why: The link really does carry 1 Gbps; one conversation cannot fill it.

choices.text: The receiver at the far end cannot process incoming data any faster than that
choices.why: Nothing here says the receiver is slow; the sender is idle waiting.

choices.text: A 64 kB window means every packet on the link is limited to 64 kB of data
choices.why: The window is how much may be unacknowledged, not the size of a packet.

choices.text: Once its window is in flight it must wait a full round trip for permission
choices.why: The pipe needs capacity × round trip in flight to stay busy.

prompt: Why is a download usually slower than a speed test on the same connection? Choose all that apply.
hint: Consider what the speed test arranged in its own favour.

choices.text: Downloads are deliberately held back by a limit in the operating system
choices.why: Nothing in the operating system caps an ordinary download.

choices.text: A speed test opens many connections at once where a download opens one
choices.why: Many windows put far more data in flight.

choices.text: The test server is chosen to be nearby, and the real one is wherever it is
choices.why: Distance costs throughput as well as latency.

choices.text: Speed tests report a figure rather larger than the one they actually measured
choices.why: They measure honestly; they measure the best case.

choices.text: The real server divides its capacity among everybody it is serving
choices.why: Your plan has no influence over the other end.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: the amount that must be in flight to keep a link busy is its capacity multiplied by the ___ ___ time.
hint: It is the delay the sender waits before permission comes back.

prompt: A 1 GB file takes 48 seconds on a 300 Mbps connection where the arithmetic says 27. Which single line of that difference is usually the largest?
hint: One of the causes is not on your side at all.

choices.text: The server dividing its capacity among everybody downloading from it
choices.why: The other end is the largest line, and your plan has no influence over it.

choices.text: Headers added at each layer, which consume most of what crosses the wire
choices.why: Overhead is a few per cent, not most.

choices.text: TCP starting cautiously and taking several seconds to reach its full rate
choices.why: Also real, and also much smaller than the other end's share.

choices.text: The difference between the advertised 300 and the delivered 280
choices.why: Real, and it is worth about two seconds of the twenty-one.

prompt: A video call breaks the moment somebody in the house starts a large download, and the download runs at full speed. What is happening?
hint: Nothing was lost, and nothing got slower.

choices.text: The call software has switched itself down to a much lower quality setting
choices.why: It may well do so, but as a response to the delay rather than its cause.

choices.text: The download is consuming all of the bandwidth that the call needed to work
choices.why: Audio is tens of kilobits per second; there was plenty left.

choices.text: Packets belonging to the call are being dropped to make room for the download
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; that is precisely why every count looks healthy.

choices.text: The router's buffer has filled, so every packet waits behind the download
choices.why: Queuing delay, which is bufferbloat — and no counter reports a problem.

prompt: Why does a router have a buffer at all?
hint: Think about what real traffic looks like second by second.

choices.text: Real traffic arrives in bursts, and a buffer stops a burst becoming a loss
choices.why: Without one, entirely normal activity would cause constant drops.

choices.text: It stores a copy of each packet in case the destination asks for it again
choices.why: Nothing in the middle keeps a copy; retransmission is the sender's job.

choices.text: It reorders the packets so that they arrive in the sequence they were sent in
choices.why: Nothing in the middle reorders anything.

choices.text: It gives the router the time it needs to read the header of each packet
choices.why: Reading a header is processing delay, and needs no buffer to hold a queue.

prompt: What single measurement identifies a bloated buffer?
hint: One number, taken at two different moments.

choices.text: The percentage of packets lost while a large download is running
choices.why: A bloated buffer is the one that does not drop anything.

choices.text: Latency measured while a large transfer is saturating the line
choices.why: 15 ms idle and 400 ms under load is a complete diagnosis.

choices.text: The advertised bandwidth compared with the delivered bandwidth
choices.why: Both can be entirely healthy while the connection is unusable for calls.

choices.text: The throughput figure reported by an ordinary speed test
choices.why: It will look perfect, which is exactly why this went unnoticed for years.

prompt: Why does queuing punish the call and not the download?
hint: The two want opposite things from the network.

choices.text: The call's packets are the smaller ones and are therefore queued last
choices.why: Position in the queue is arrival order, not size.

choices.text: Calls are carried over UDP, which routers handle with less care than TCP
choices.why: Routers read the destination and do not know which transport is inside.

choices.text: The download wants throughput and tolerates delay; the call is the reverse
choices.why: A single first-come-first-served line serves the one that caused it.

choices.text: The download is given priority by the router over other traffic
choices.why: An ordinary queue has no priorities; it is first come, first served.

prompt: Which of these genuinely help with bufferbloat? Choose all that apply.
hint: One popular answer makes no difference at all.

choices.text: Smart queue management, keeping separate lines and serving each a little
choices.why: A burst of voice never sits behind a download.

choices.text: Buying a connection with considerably more bandwidth on it
choices.why: A wider line fills more slowly and then does exactly the same thing.

choices.text: Increasing the size of the buffer the router keeps for each of its links
choices.why: That is what caused it: a bigger buffer holds a longer queue.

choices.text: Restarting the router whenever a call starts going bad
choices.why: It clears the queue for a moment and the download refills it immediately.

choices.text: Configuring the connection slightly below its true capacity
choices.why: The buffer that is causing it — often the provider's — then never fills.

prompt: Two connections have the same average latency, but one delivers packets at even intervals and the other in bunches. What is the difference called?
hint: It is variation rather than magnitude.

choices.text: Throughput
choices.why: That is the rate real data moved, and it could be identical for both.

choices.text: Loss
choices.why: Loss is packets never arriving; here everything arrives.

choices.text: Propagation delay
choices.why: That is distance, and it is the same for both here.

choices.text: Jitter
choices.why: Live audio has to be played at a constant rate, so variation is what hurts it.

prompt: Why does a receiver keep a jitter buffer, and what does it cost?
hint: It is the same trade as the previous section, on a smaller scale.

choices.text: It compresses the audio so that it fits through a smaller connection
choices.why: A jitter buffer holds timing, not quality.

choices.text: It stores arriving packets so that lost ones can be requested a second time
choices.why: Live audio does not ask for anything again; there would be no time.

choices.text: It reorders packets, at the cost of processing on the receiver
choices.why: Reordering is not the problem; arriving unevenly is.

choices.text: It gives late packets room to arrive, and adds its own delay to every word
choices.why: Applications grow and shrink it constantly as the network changes.

prompt: A link loses 2% of packets. Why does a download slow down far more than 2%?
hint: Ask what TCP concludes when a packet goes missing.

choices.text: Lost packets are sent again at a lower priority than data that is still new
choices.why: Nothing assigns priorities; it is the rate reduction that costs.

choices.text: Loss is the only congestion signal there is, so TCP keeps reducing its rate
choices.why: The sender spends its life backing off and cautiously recovering.

choices.text: A 2% loss rate means 2% of the connection's whole capacity becomes unusable
choices.why: If that were all, the effect would indeed be about 2%.

choices.text: Each lost packet must be sent three times before it gets through
choices.why: One retransmission usually suffices; the cost is the slowing down.

prompt: Match each complaint to the number that explains it.
hint: Two of them are about time rather than about capacity.

pairs.left: The call breaks only when somebody downloads
Everything feels sluggish but files arrive fine

right_distractors: The narrowest link on the path

prompt: Where does packet loss usually come from? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of these are far more common than the rest.

choices.text: Routers along the way discarding traffic they consider to be low priority
choices.why: An ordinary router reads a destination and has no view about the content.

choices.text: A buffer that has actually run out of room
choices.why: Loss and bloat are the same event at different stages.

choices.text: Something physical — a damaged cable, a connector, interference
choices.why: A corrupted frame is discarded in silence.

choices.text: A congested link somewhere in the middle at a particular hour
choices.why: Recognisable because it appears at the same time every day.

choices.text: The destination machine refusing packets that it was not expecting to receive
choices.why: That produces an immediate refusal, not silent loss.

prompt: Match each complaint to the number that explains it.
hint: One of these is about the other end rather than about your line.

pairs.left: A download is slower than the plan promises
The voice is choppy and keeps cutting
Large files take too long, everything else is fine

prompt: A plan is sold as 1 Gbps. About how many megabytes per second should a download show?
hint: Divide by eight.

prompt: A site is slow. A speed test on the same machine reports the full advertised figure. What has the speed test told you?
hint: Ask what it measured, and to where.

choices.text: That the connection has enough bandwidth, so latency cannot be the issue
choices.why: Latency is precisely what a bandwidth measurement does not cover.

choices.text: That your line to a nearby server is healthy, and nothing about that site
choices.why: Distance, the other end and latency are all outside what it measured.

choices.text: That the problem must therefore be somewhere inside the browser itself
choices.why: It could be the distance, the server, or queuing — none of them the browser.

choices.text: That the site must be deliberately limiting what it sends to your connection
choices.why: Far more ordinary explanations come first.

prompt: Put the events of bufferbloat in order.
hint: Nothing is lost at any point in this sequence.
items: A download begins and increases its rate, looking for a limit
More arrives at the router than the outgoing link can carry
The excess goes into the buffer, which fills and stays full
A voice packet arrives and joins the back of a very long queue
The call degrades while every counter still reports success
trap: The common swap is putting the loss before the delay — a bloated buffer is precisely the one that does not drop anything, which is why nothing reports a problem.

prompt: Which pair of measurements together identify a bloated buffer?
hint: One number, twice, under different conditions.

choices.text: Throughput measured on one connection, and then on eight of them at once
choices.why: That tells you about windows, not about queues.

choices.text: Latency when the line is idle, and latency while it is saturated
choices.why: 15 ms against 400 ms is the whole diagnosis.

choices.text: The loss percentage when idle, and the loss percentage under a full load
choices.why: A bloated buffer is the one that avoids loss by queueing instead.

choices.text: The bandwidth that was advertised, and the bandwidth actually delivered
choices.why: Both can be perfect while calls are unusable.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: a bigger buffer trades ___ for ___, which is why a download is unharmed and a call is ruined.
hint: The download gets one of these and the call needed the other.

prompt: Why does putting a copy of content closer to the user help, when the user's bandwidth is unchanged?
hint: Two of this lesson's numbers improve at once.

choices.text: It compresses the content beforehand so that less of it has to travel
choices.why: A copy nearby is the same content, in a nearer place.

choices.text: It increases the amount of bandwidth that is available to that user
choices.why: The user's line is exactly as wide as it was.

choices.text: It cuts the round trip, which shortens the waiting and lifts the rate
choices.why: Distance costs both latency and throughput, and a copy nearby reduces both.

choices.text: It removes the need for anything on the connection to be acknowledged
choices.why: Acknowledgement still happens; it simply comes back sooner.

prompt: A traceroute shows 180 ms at hop six and 40 ms at hop seven. What should you conclude?
hint: Ask where those replies come from and what produces them.

choices.text: The path happened to change in between the two separate probes
choices.why: Possible, but the ordinary explanation is the router deprioritising its reply.

choices.text: Little — a router treats answering these probes as its least important work
choices.why: A high number at one hop that falls at the next is the router being busy, not the path.

choices.text: Hop six is congested and is therefore the cause of the slowness
choices.why: If hop six really delayed traffic, hop seven could not be faster.

choices.text: Hop six is dropping a share of the packets that reach it
choices.why: Nothing here indicates loss; it indicates a slow reply.

prompt: Which of these change how a page *feels* to load, rather than how long a large file takes? Choose all that apply.
hint: Small transfers and large ones are limited by different things.

choices.text: Reducing the round trip between the browser and the server
choices.why: Most of a small page load is waiting, and every wait is a round trip.

choices.text: Removing the queuing delay on a line that is saturated
choices.why: It is latency, and it is often the largest component of it.

choices.text: Serving the content from somewhere considerably nearer
choices.why: The same as reducing the round trip, arranged differently.

choices.text: Increasing the size of the buffer the router keeps for each of its links
choices.why: That lengthens the waiting rather than shortening it.

choices.text: Doubling the bandwidth of the connection
choices.why: It shortens the transfer, which for a small page was already short.

prompt: Sending a large file feels far slower than receiving one of the same size. Why?
hint: The plan has two numbers, and one of them is rarely advertised.

choices.text: Sending needs an acknowledgement per packet where receiving does not
choices.why: Both directions are acknowledged in the same way.

choices.text: Encryption is applied to what you send and not to what you receive
choices.why: Encryption applies in both directions.

choices.text: Domestic connections are asymmetric — upload is a fraction of download
choices.why: 300 down and 30 up is an ordinary pairing.

choices.text: The server at the far end accepts data more slowly than it sends it
choices.why: Sometimes true, and far less often the explanation than the plan's own asymmetry.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: on a long path, distance costs you not only latency but also ___, because one conversation can only keep so much data in ___.
hint: The second word is where data sits between being sent and being acknowledged.

prompt: Somebody says their internet is slow. What is the first thing worth establishing?
hint: The word covers at least five different measurements.

choices.text: Which of the numbers they mean — files, pages, calls or something else
choices.why: The five have different causes and different fixes, and the word covers all of them.

choices.text: Whether they have paid for enough bandwidth on their current plan
choices.why: Bandwidth is one of five candidates and frequently not the one.

choices.text: Whether the equipment they are using needs to be replaced
choices.why: A guess at a fix before the symptom has been identified.

choices.text: Whether other people in the same building happen to be online
choices.why: A reasonable question once you know which number is wrong, not before.
